source.title: LCDB 1.1: A Database Illustrating Learning Curves Are More Ill-Behaved Than Previously Thought
source.authors: Chen Yan; F. Mohr; Tom J. Viering

record.tranche_reason: The study measures sample-wise classification-error curves and reports peaking and other increases in error as training-set size grows. This is a conceptual test of the more-data-can-hurt aspect, using a different setup and not testing model-capacity double descent.
record.gate_note: The paper focuses exclusively on sample-wise learning curves for tabular classification. Its reported percentages aggregate curves over learners and datasets; they do not locate peaks relative to an interpolation threshold. Epoch-wise curves, model-size sweeps, and results cited from other work are not results of this study. Validation-set error is used for the main shape analyses.
record.test_reason: The study measures sample-wise validation-error curves for 24+ tabular learners and detects peaking, which it calls sample-wise double descent. For LDA, it locates the peak at training-set size ≈ dimensionality, the interpolation threshold of the pseudo-inverse Fisher classifier. This is a new setting (classical tabular learners) with results on V3. It does not vary capacity or epochs.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct: about 15% (14.9%) of CC-18 no-FS curves are significantly ill-behaved, and feature scaling rarely fixes it and sometimes worsens it. Ill-behavior hurts curve fitting, and crossing curves hurt successive halving. The paraphrase should add that peaking concentrates in Fisher-related learners (LDA, Ridge), with the LDA peak at n ≈ d as peaking literature predicts.
record.recipe_differences: The study builds and analyzes a database of sample-wise curves across tabular learners and datasets, using validation error and statistical tests; it does not reproduce deep-network capacity or epoch sweeps from the cited double-descent studies.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature scaling changes the reported prevalence of non-monotonicity, peaking, and dipping; the effect differs across learners. The authors report that scaling marginally reduces overall ill-behavior, while some learners become more ill-behaved and others improve.

fits_no_version.finding: About 6–10% of learning curves are significantly non-monotone or dip: more data worsens error without recovery. Sigmoid SVM, Naive Bayes, Nearest Centroid and KNN are mainly responsible, unrelated to any interpolation threshold.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: More training data can raise validation error in classical tabular learners through dipping, independent of an interpolation threshold.

record.peer_reviewed: NeurIPS 2025 Track on Datasets and Benchmarks
record.problems: The main analysis uses validation rather than test error and is scoped to tabular classification. Peak location relative to an interpolation threshold is not analyzed. The authors note that detected ill-behavior can depend on curve length and on conservative statistical-testing choices; a few LDA/QDA curves are non-reproducible, and QDA is excluded from analysis.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed per-learner breakdowns in Table 3, Tables 6–8, and Appendix D, along with figure-level curve examples and additional scaling-specific learner analyses, are not enumerated here; the included Table 4 aggregates directly quantify the sample-wise error increases relevant to V3. Table 8 is flattened in the supplied text, so its individual entries were not assigned to learners.

untested.parts: No epoch-wise curves; the study explicitly excludes them.
Test-set error (validation error is used), deep networks near their own interpolation threshold, and threshold location for learners other than LDA.
No capacity sweeps past an interpolation point.
No effective-complexity measure is tested across size, epochs or samples.
No label-noise manipulation, no multiple-descent analysis, no tuned regularization (hyperparameter tuning left to future work).

missing.what: Per-learner peaking rates: LDA 37.5% (CC-18) / 24.5% (FULL) in all scalings; Ridge 13.9% no FS, 1.4% min-max, 12.5% std; MLP 8.3% no FS vs 0% std; SVM_RBF 6.9%.
MLP peaks line up at specific sizes caused by a tiny final mini-batch; they vanish under standardization, so they are an artifact rather than threshold peaking.
LDA peaking is underestimated because about 15% of CC-18 datasets have fewer than 16 features, below the first anchor.

record.verdict_notes: Table 4's first three columns are CC-18 and the next three are FULL; the record copied CC-18 values into several FULL rows. Tranche changed to T3 because this is a learning-curve shape survey on classical tabular learners, not a method aimed at double descent. All curves use validation error.

versions.untested_parts: Model size, deep-network scaling, and peak location relative to the size that just fits the training set.
The relation of peaks to an interpolation threshold; test-set rather than validation-set error; deep-network-specific settings.
Capacity sweeps across model classes and descent beyond an interpolation point. The study varies training-set size, not capacity.
A unified effective-complexity measure across size, epochs, and sample count. The study reports only an LDA peak-location comparison with dataset dimensionality.
Whether label noise or variance drives peaks, whether multiple descent peaks occur, and whether optimally tuned regularization removes them.
Whether recounting complexity as an effective parameter count turns second descent into a U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: LDA
rows.operation_detail: Compared the estimated sample-size location of LDA peaks with dataset dimensionality.
rows.value: Peak occurs at a training-set size approximately equal to dimensionality
rows.note: This is a single-axis, learner-specific association, not a unified effective-complexity account.
rows.check: Mislinked to V5. A peak at n ≈ d for LDA is a peak at the sample-wise interpolation threshold, so it bears on V3. It is a single-learner, single-axis finding and does not test a unified complexity measure.

relationships.condition: LDA (Fisher-type linear classifier) on LCDB 1.1 CC-18, all scalings
relationships.reason: Validation error peaks at training-set size ≈ dimensionality, then recovers with more data (r22). Per-learner Table 8 gives LDA peaking in 37.5% of CC-18 curves (text-based, see missing).
relationships.display_finding: Validation error peaked near training-set size equal to dimensionality and then recovered, with peaking reported in 37.5% of CC-18 curves.

source_check.reason: Appendix E.4 and Figure 14a place the LDA peak near n ≈ d and report invariance to feature scaling; Table 8 reports 37.5% peaking for CC-18 under each scaling.

relationships.condition: Aggregate across all tabular learners and scalings
relationships.reason: Pooled peaking rates are at or below the 5% false-positive bound (r2, r5, r8, r14, r17, r20), and only marginally above it for FULL no-FS (r11). Sample-wise peaking is confined to a few learners (LDA, Ridge, some MLP). Per the text, MLP peaks are a mini-batch artifact removed by standardization, and Ridge peaking largely disappears under min-max scaling.
relationships.display_finding: Pooled peaking rates stay at or below the 5% false-positive bound except for one marginal exceedance; peaks occur in LDA, Ridge, and some MLPs, with standardization removing MLP mini-batch artifacts and min-max scaling largely removing Ridge peaks.
